rss_0_1793053611.title: Nerve activity initiates autoimmune hair loss
rss_0_1793053611.text:
“I’m as free as my hair,” proclaims the pop star Lady Gaga in her song ‘Hair’. Indeed, hair can be a statement of freedom and it informs our sense of self. Conversely, baldness (a condition called alopecia) can be considered an attack on the self, not only in a psychological sense, but also in a literal sense through autoimmunity, in which immune cells that usually ignore the body’s own tissues instead damage organs and cause problems such as hair loss. Writing in Nature, Cui et al.1 provide insights into autoimmune hair loss from their studies of mice.

Nature 658, 1131-1132 (2026)

rss_1_1793053612.title: Women might have invented language — but not alone
rss_1_1793053612.text:
The Revolutionary Origins of Language Chris Knight & Jerome Lewis Yale Univ. Press (2026)

The origins of writing and script remain unclear, but those of speech and language are simply unknown. This is because no physical evidence remains of the earliest language, which was probably spoken in Africa, the birthplace of Homo sapiens. By contrast, inscribed marks on clay tablets that constitute the earliest known form of writing — however mysterious — have survived from ancient Mesopotamia, dating to the fourth millennium bc.

Humanity spoke thousands of languages at the dawn of farming — now many of them are lost

That’s left a lot of room for scholars to speculate on how speech and language began, starting with thinkers from the ancient world, including Plato, who could not decide whether language had a natural or a purely human origin. By the nineteenth century, anthropologists had grown tired of so much talk with scant evidence to go on.

In 1866, the founding statutes of the Paris Linguistic Society forbade all discussion of the subject, note anthropologists Chris Knight and Jerome Lewis in The Revolutionary Origins of Language. “Anyone theorizing about the origins of language risked being dismissed as a crank.” Even so, “from time to time, this or that brave maverick would risk whatever reputation they had by attempting to reopen the debate”.

Science of linguistics

The best known, if controversial, attempts since then come from linguist Noam Chomsky, starting in the 1960s. The authors discuss his contributions at length, drawing on Knight’s book Decoding Chomsky (2016).

How the world’s largest language family spread — and why others go extinct

In 1987, Chomsky remarked in Language and Problems of Knowledge that: “There is a long history of study of the origin of language, asking how it came from the calls of apes and so forth.” But, in his view, this investigation is a “complete waste of time”.

That’s because language is based on “an entirely different principle than any animal communication system”, he wrote. Although human gestures might have evolved from animal communication systems, the same could not apply to human language, Chomsky thought.

This view was supported by an academic study, launched in 1973, of a young chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes) with the punning name Nim Chimpsky. Nim learnt from his human supervisors how to make dozens of hand signs to procure food and other rewards, but not how to communicate in American Sign Language or to speak a language. “Give orange me give eat orange me eat orange give me eat orange give me you” was Nim’s longest recorded sign-language sequence, as cited by Knight and Lewis.

Nim Chimpsky the chimpanzee was taught how to make hand signs for food and other rewards.Credit: Mel Finkelstein/NY Daily News Archive/Getty

In Chomsky’s view, human language arose suddenly because of a single genetic mutation, not from Darwinian natural selection or through a gradual, adaptive cultural process. In other words, argue the authors, by declaring language to be “an especially intriguing and mysterious aspect of the natural world, to be investigated using the normal methods of natural science”, Chomsky elevated the study of linguistics to a scientific challenge in the field of anthropology.

However, they add, “there is no measuring device, magnifying glass, telescope or other instrument which can grasp the meaning of a word.” So how can conventional science investigate language?

Social origins

Rejecting Chomsky’s view, Knight and Lewis instead offer a complex mixture of evidence, both scientific and cultural, to support their own theory. This evidence is mostly drawn from prehistoric and present-day Africa, where Lewis spent three decades studying hunter-gatherers, notably the BaYaka people in Central Africa.

“To qualify as science, a hypothesis must suggest testable predictions,” the authors remark. Given that there can be no direct evidence for events in the distant past, scientists must therefore “construct tests from a wide range of telltale clues”. These include: “recurrent structures of magical myth, initiation rituals, hunters’ taboos, patterns of menstrual prohibition, lunar and solar influences, and critically, archaeological evidence for symbolism in the form of red ochre pigments and personal ornaments”. All of these clues are examined in their intriguing, if rambling, book.

AI is helping to decode animals’ speech. Will it also let us talk with them?

Although anthropologists have often suggested that speech and language arose from hunting or warfare, Knight and Lewis refute these two theories. While hunting in the forest, male hunter-gatherers “do their utmost to avoid having to speak aloud”, so as to lure animals towards them. Instead, they use sign language to alert each other to the nearby presence of animals such as gorillas, antelopes, leopards and elephants.

rss_2_1793053613.title: Are salaries getting worse? Many scientists think so
rss_2_1793053613.text:
Nature’s 2026 job satisfaction survey This article is the second in a series discussing the results of Nature’s 2026 science-job satisfaction survey. It’s the latest edition of such surveys, which started in 2010; the last two took place in 2018 and 2021. The 2026 survey, created in partnership with Thinks Insight & Strategy, a research consultancy in London, launched in May and was advertised on nature.com, in Springer Nature digital products and through e-mail campaigns. It had 3,882 self-selecting respondents across 133 countries with 31% describing themselves as female and 19% as belonging to a minority ethnic group in their country of work. The full survey data sets are available at go.nature.com/4b2drrc.

Umar, a mathematics lecturer in northern Nigeria, has worked at his university for more than ten years. In that time, he’s had only one pay rise: in 2024, when the government raised the national minimum wage. With no inflation- or promotion-based adjustments, his income no longer covers his basic living costs. Instead, he has to borrow money, take on extra jobs and cut back on essential spending. “Unfortunately, my experience is not an isolated one” for Nigerian scientists, he says.

On the other side of the Atlantic Ocean, Ashley — an early-career physicist employed on a fixed-term contract in a university in the eastern United States — says she is much worse off than her parents, neither of whom have degrees. “It’s really messed up that I have a job that requires a PhD in science, yet I’m paid US$20,000 less per year than my father earned at his job 20 years ago, before accounting for inflation.” Ashley lists the things she can’t afford, including children (her pay won’t cover childcare, nor putting them through university) and home ownership. She thinks she did everything ‘right’ — for example, having jobs alongside her undergraduate studies to avoid debt. “Yet I am still locked out of the middle-class existence I have worked myself half to death for,” she says, adding: “It sucks. It really, really sucks.”

Umar and Ashley (not their real names) live in countries with vastly different resources for research and costs of living. But their stories reflect a global theme. When Nature’s careers team surveyed them and nearly 4,000 other scientists earlier this year about their salaries, less than half said they had received a pay rise in the past 12 months. Around one-third said that their salaries covered only basic expenses, and one in ten said their income failed to do even that.

The survey asked respondents to convert their gross (before-taxes) salary into US dollars, then choose the range into which it falls. More than half earn less than US$50,000 a year, and 22% make at least $80,000. In 2021, when Nature last ran this survey, 38% earned below $50,000 and 32% earned $80,000 or more. But this apparent drop in global salaries might be because of geographical shifts in those surveyed — particularly a rise in respondents from Asia, who made up 10% in 2021 and 39% this year. From continents with enough respondents for comparison, North American scientists earn the most, followed by those in Europe, then Asia (see ‘The scientist’s wallet’).

Industry salaries exceed those in academia by 66%, and more scientists in industry are satisfied with their salary (58%) than are those in academia (43%). But even in the private sector, some think that they should earn more. “It feels like I’m making less and less every year,” says a researcher working at a biomedical technology company in a large city in the midwestern United States, who, like many scientists Nature spoke to, asked to remain anonymous when discussing pay concerns.

She moved from working at a university to her current job four years ago after discovering that she was pregnant, because she judged childcare expenses to be unaffordable on her previous salary. But despite having a dozen years of work experience in both industry and academia, she says that she is still paid like a recent graduate.

“I love science and what I do, but I also feel undervalued,” she says.

Purchasing power

Scientists in the United States earn the most out of the ten countries in the survey that had more than 100 respondents, which means the results from these nations can be compared sensibly. Some 65% of United States-based scientists report earning more than $80,000 a year. The lowest wages are found in India, where 53% earn less than $15,000 a year. Comparing continents, the lowest salaries are found in Africa, where 61% earn below $15,000 per year.

We need to talk about salaries in science

However, the survey’s self-reported salary figures in converted US dollars do not reflect what those incomes can buy on the ground. A dollar buys more in India than in the United States: nearly five times more. According to purchasing-power calculations by the International Monetary Fund, a $15,000 salary in India is comparable to a $70,000 salary in the United States. When adjusted for purchasing power, average salaries in the survey for Canada overtake those in the United States, salaries in Germany come close to US ones and the wide salary gaps between emerging economies and wealthier nations shrink. And it’s important to note that a nation’s average salary in the survey can be skewed by sample biases with respect to factors such as location within a nation, employment sector and career stage.

In Brazil, where 21% of respondents report earning less than $15,000, a low or modest salary by US or western-European standards can “provide a reasonably comfortable life locally”, especially outside the most expensive cities such as Rio de Janeiro or Sao Paolo, says Haroldo Ribeiro, a physicist at the State University of Maringá in Brazil. “Still, I would not conclude that Brazilian scientists are generally well paid,” he says. Although salaries in public universities there have increased in the past few years, this comes after a long period of stagnation, he says, making it a recovery, not a raise.

Strings attached

Only 44% of people in the total sample are satisfied with their pay, but this varies between countries. Significantly more scientists in Canada (61%), Germany (68%) and the United States (55%) are satisfied with their income than the global average. The countries with at least 100 respondents that had the lowest numbers of scientists satisfied with their salary are Turkey (27%), China (39%) and Italy (40%).

China’s lower-than-average satisfaction with salary comes despite survey data suggesting that Chinese salaries have risen in US-dollar terms since Nature asked scientists the same question in 2021. Some 11% of Chinese respondents reported earning more than $80,000 this year, nearly doubling from 6% in 2021. Over the same time, in the United Kingdom, the proportion earning more than $80,000 grew from 19% to only 22%.

Salaries can vary substantially between China’s economically developed coastal areas, and its more-sparsely populated west, as well as between universities, says survey respondent Jingrui Sun, a freshwater ecologist at Yunnan University in Kunming, China. He describes his salary as “sufficient for me to live comfortably”, and says that it is common for research-intensive universities and institutions in wealthy parts of the country to offer employees performance-related pay, as well as housing subsidies and laboratory start-up packages.

But good salaries in China come with extra demands, Sun says. “Part of the package is linked to periodic assessments, and if the required targets are not met, remuneration in the following period can be reduced substantially.” He says a few of his colleagues have had their pay docked this year, after their university introduced more-stringent assessment criteria. “Such changes can have real consequences for staff retention, and have prompted academics to leave and take positions at other institutions,” he says.

Falling behind

Annual pay rises are not the global norm, the survey shows. Only 45% of respondents say they had received a raise in the previous 12 months, and 6% report a cut in pay. Industry researchers are more likely than the average result to have had a pay rise (54%), whereas the opposite is true for those who earn less than $50,000 a year (42% of whom received one).

Many survey-takers are frustrated that they aren’t getting paid more. One non-tenure-track US researcher who works in a biology department says that she exceeds her department’s tenure criteria and outperforms several of her tenure-track colleagues. Those colleagues are paid at least $20,000 more than her annually and get more research funding. “Yet my department chairs keep looking me dead in the eye and saying there’s no appetite for raises” for people like her, she says.

What’s the secret sauce for happy scientists at work? These eight countries offer some clues

When salaries grow, it’s often not enough. One researcher with a fixed-term contract in Pune, India, says his public-sector salary has not kept up with “skyrocketing urban inflation” in the city of seven million people. He says that rent, public transport and groceries consume most of his pay. “At this salary, no one can even think of home or car loans,” he says. Add a child, he says, and “it’s just a matter of survival”.

In Europe, where 27% of respondents report earning more than $80,000 a year, salaries vary massively between countries, says Norbert Bencze, president of Eurodoc, an organization for early-career researchers in Europe. “A good salary in the Netherlands is something very different from a good salary in Poland or Hungary.” However, living costs outpacing pay increases are a common problem across the continent, he says. “Some researchers have seen their actual purchasing power fall quite radically, in some cases cut in half over the past ten years, even though they got regular pay rises.” Although Nature’s salary survey was of post-PhD researchers and lab technicians, Eurodoc’s survey of doctoral pay in 2025 showed that PhD students earned below minimum wage in five European countries: Hungary, Ireland, Poland, Romania and Ukraine (see go.nature.com/4s7m1tu).

Fairer, more transparent salary-setting would be welcome, even if scientists’ wages continue to underwhelm, survey participants say. “It is not only about paying more, but about making compensation feel clear, consistent and linked to contribution,” says a materials scientist in India. People should understand how salaries are decided, what the path to a raise or promotion looks like and whether their pay is competitive with the market, he says.

Researchers who had not taken the survey felt similarly when Nature spoke to them about the results. In Portugal, academic salaries have risen in recent years, mainly to keep up with inflation, says Ronaldo Sousa, an aquatic ecologist at the Interdisciplinary Centre of Marine and Environmental Research near Porto. However, to get a pay rise that is substantially above inflation, scientists must move up the academic ladder, for example from assistant professor to associate professor. “We might publish a dozen high-impact papers in a year, but this will not necessarily result in any increase in salary,” he says.

rss_3_1793053615.title: Can science make your dog live longer? Longevity craze comes to pets
rss_3_1793053615.text:
Not just for humans: gene therapy to extend longevity is under investigation for dogs, too.Credit: Juliana Yamada/Los Angeles Times/Getty

Vera Gorbunova has attended many a longevity conference over her decades of studying ageing. But never one quite like this.

Earlier this month, Gorbunova, a researcher at Rochester University in New York, joined scientists from industry and academia — and a fair few of their dogs — for the Animal Longevity Summit in Toronto, Canada. Given it was the inaugural summit, it was small. But it highlighted a growing interest in the science of extending the lifespan of pets.

On the agenda were presentations by academic researchers such as Gorbunova, who studies ageing in various animal species. Others presented projects about understanding cancer in dogs, regeneration in axolotls and the genetics of mammals that thrive in extreme environments. Alongside the university scientists were researchers at companies pursuing gene therapies for dogs, probiotic kibble for cats, and cryopreservation of pets.

Big dogs age faster than little ones — rogue ‘jumping genes’ might be to blame

“It was maybe a somewhat different crowd of people than you see at the typical ageing conferences,” Gorbunova says.

The conference reflected a market reality: as the pursuit of increasing human longevity and healthspan has grown, fuelled by hefty investment, it only stands to reason that some of that interest would spill over to pets, says Cameron Hurlburt, a senior analyst at Ani VC, a venture-capital firm in Miami, Florida. The US pet- and animal-health market is estimated to be worth US$150 billion and could grow as more people in the United States purchase pet health insurance, he says.

Muscle for moggies

Most of the current efforts to promote longer pet healthspans focus on improving animal diets, including probiotic formulations, Hurlburt says. And when it comes to therapies, many companies are looking to repurpose drugs that are already approved for humans, rather than starting from scratch.

But not everyone is taking that approach. The Cat Health Company in Bucharest presented its strategy for identifying new drugs for ageing-associated diseases in cats, including a muscle-wasting condition called sarcopenia, and kidney disease. The company has two compounds in clinical trials now, with others on the way, says Alex Băciţa, co-founder and chief operating officer of the company.

How ageing changes our genes — huge epigenetic atlas gives clearest picture yet

Others are venturing into gene therapies. Rejuvenate Bio, a biotechnology company in San Diego, California, is working on one to treat mitral valve disease, the most common heart condition in dogs. But co-founder and chief scientific officer Noah Davidsohn hopes that this will be just the first use for the therapy, and that the same treatment will eventually be used to treat metabolic syndromes and improve longevity. Rejuvenate has worked to decrease the cost of manufacturing gene therapies, which are complex treatments, to a level that would be compatible with the pet market.

Another company, called Genflow Biosciences, is pursuing a gene therapy to enhance longevity and reduce sarcopenia in dogs. If the drug shows success, the company hopes to sell it to a larger animal-health company, and then use the proceeds to help to fund studies of the same approach in humans, says Eric Leire, founder and chief executive of the firm in Brussels.

Academic researchers also stand to gain by interacting with the latest companies to spring up, said Noah Snyder-Mackler, a comparative geroscientist at Arizona State University in Tempe, before the meeting. Government grants for studying dogs often focus on applying the results to human health, rather than canine health. That means that academic researchers might need to collaborate with industry to conduct studies that lead to treatments for dogs.

“We don’t have the resources to follow up with dog-centric interventions,” says Snyder-Mackler, a researcher on the Dog Aging Project, a large collaboration to study ageing in pooches. Gorbunova says she enjoyed the meeting. “It was a revelation to me to see how interested people are in extending the life of their pets,” she says.

rss_5_1793053617.title: Evolutionary ‘game-changer’: weird armoured amphibian lived in ancient seas
rss_5_1793053617.text:
A newly discovered amphibian species called Gerrothorax maritimus was about 74 centimetres long and had a flattened, armoured body.Credit: Ryosuke Motani

Amphibians were able to live in the sea 237 million years ago, according to research published today in Nature Ecology & Evolution1.

Two fossils of a type of primitive amphibian from a group called temnospondyls were found in what is now Guizhou province in China — which would have been a salty sea during the Late Triassic period. The researchers have provisionally named the species Gerrothorax maritimus. The 74-centimetre-long creatures had flattened bodies and were almost completely covered in body armour.

There are more than 8,000 modern amphibian species, but none of them lives exclusively in a marine environment. “This is potentially a revolutionary discovery,” says Steve Brusatte, a palaeontologist and evolutionary biologist at the University of Edinburgh, UK. “If this Triassic amphibian, Gerrothorax, really was fully marine, then it is a game-changer.”

Schematic of one of the amphibian fossils, colour-coded on the basis of skeletal parts, and with bones labelled.Credit: Diao, L. et al./Nature Ecol. Evol.

Amphibians have varying levels of salt tolerance, says Ryosuke Motani, a palaeobiologist at the University of California, Davis, and a co-author of the study. But even salt-tolerant animals need to recover from excess salt in one way or another, he explains. “In most cases, they do it by drinking fresh water.”

Salt slurpers

The researchers argue that this was not an option for G. maritimus: the excellent preservation of the skeletons, so far from any land mass that existed at the time, suggests that they were not swept there by water. The team also measured isotopes of the element strontium, which can help to date minerals and water in marine samples. The levels in the ancient animals’ bones matched those in the seawater at the time, which suggests that the creatures “grew up drinking the seawater”, the researchers write in the paper.

rss_6_1793053619.title: The Selfish Gene, 50 years on — it’s time for an update
rss_6_1793053619.text:
I first read The Selfish Gene in the 1980s, as a graduate student in neurobiology and animal behaviour. I admired the clarity with which biologist Richard Dawkins distilled mid-twentieth-century work in evolutionary biology.

The idea at the core of the book, published in 1976, was thrillingly simple: that a living organism is just a gene’s way of making more organisms that can carry the gene down the generations.

Dawkins’s paradox: dissecting the body’s battle to keep selfish genes in check

Back then, The Selfish Gene seemed pretty harmless. Dawkins’s ideas tracked with mainstream sociobiology. It was a popular book that covered exactly the sort of ideas that my lecturers were already teaching.

Re-reading it now, with decades of scholarship in the history of biology under my belt, it seems less benign. The determinism baked into the “gene’s-eye view” in the book troubles me, as does the passivity of the organism in Dawkins’s telling — a “vehicle”, a mere “replicator”. The implication: that traits such as aggression are hard-wired into people. Fortunately, over the past couple of decades, new tools, fresh models and scholars in many disciplines have begun to embrace the complex reality of biology. Readers in search of an understanding of life on Earth today would do better to reach for books that take a broader view.

Gene-centric views

The Selfish Gene was the apotheosis of the ‘modern evolutionary synthesis’. That theory uses mathematics to quantify species evolution at the population level, through changes in the frequency of different versions of genes, known as alleles, across time and space.

Dawkins wrote in The Selfish Gene that the gene’s-eye view was “implicit” in the 1930s writings of modern-synthesis pioneer (and eugenicist) Ronald Fisher and his contemporaries, but was made “explicit” by evolutionary biologists George Williams and William Hamilton, in the 1960s. “For me,” he wrote, “their insight had a visionary quality. But I found their expressions of it too laconic, not full-throated enough.” The Selfish Gene, then, takes the ideas to their extreme.

Richard Dawkins book of the dead is haunted by ghosts of past works

The modern synthesis blends two branches of evolutionary biology and genetics: neo-Darwinian evolution and Mendelian genetics. Neo-Darwinian evolution was established in the 1890s by biologist August Weismann in his book Die Keimplasma (The Germ Plasm). The book builds off On the Origin of Species, in which Charles Darwin outlines a central tenet — organisms evolve over many generations through an internal process called natural selection. This is the Darwinism of the first edition of On the Origin of Species, published in 1859. Yet over five successive editions, published between then and 1872, Darwin had given increasing credence to the ‘effects of use and disuse’ — the idea, associated with naturalist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, that characteristics acquired during an organism’s lifetime can be inherited. Darwin wrote, for example, about blind cave fish (Astyanax mexicanus). Their ancestors had eyes when they first nosed into a lightless cave. But after going unused for generations, the eyes degenerated, and the change gradually became heritable.

Darwin saw no reason that his theories couldn’t accommodate such phenomena. He didn’t speculate on mechanisms. Today, an evolutionary biologist might argue that any animal that put less energy than its neighbours into making a complex but useless structure, such as an unused eye, would have surplus energy to devote to, say, bigger gonads or defending its territory, and thus would gain a survival advantage. To Weismann, however, incorporating use and disuse into Darwinism was a dangerous move towards teleology, and risked ceding biological change to bishops and mystics. He proposed that only the germ plasm (the material carried in sperm and egg cells) was passed from parents to offspring. Nothing outside could affect what was transmitted.

Trays containing the entire human genome, split into more than 20,000 fragments of DNA.Credit: James King-Holmes/SPL

The second field that makes up the modern synthesis, Mendelian genetics, was invented not by Gregor Mendel, the nineteenth-century monk after whom the field is named, but by naturalist William Bateson, in his strange and brilliant 1902 book, Mendel’s Principles of Heredity: A Defence. Mendel ran experiments crossing peas, and in 1866 published a paper describing rules that governed how traits were passed down — how many offspring of a green and yellow pea cross would be green and how many yellow, for instance. We now know that only some traits, controlled by single genes, follow the simplistic patterns he observed.

The conservative Mendel claimed only to have found a law “valid for Pisum” (the pea genus); Bateson claimed that all heredity followed Mendel’s laws. Bateson’s book was ‘a defence’ against the theories of his rival and erstwhile best friend, Walter Weldon, who argued that such neat, simple laws do not describe how nature works. Weldon pointed out that traits such as height vary continuously, in a bell-shaped, normal distribution. He argued that such traits result from many factors, both hereditary and environmental.

In the end, as historian Gregory Radick has argued, Mendelism became the universally accepted form of heredity more for practical reasons than because it captured an essential truth. It’s easy to teach and methodologically simple.

The new biology

Both components of the modern synthesis focus on the gene as the sole determinant of heredity. Both halves reached essentially universal acceptance well before Dawkins came along — the spit and swagger of the field’s proponents keeping challenges and alternatives at bay.

To a historian, this universal acceptance sounds close to ideology. Fortunately, since The Selfish Gene was published, scientists’ understanding of the basic mechanisms that drive evolution has changed drastically.

rss_7_1793053620.title: Mentoring a lab colleague? Share your ‘CV of failures’ with them
rss_7_1793053620.text:
Alena Vdovchenko 00:04

So I’m a chemist and experimental scientist, so I don’t need to search very hard for examples of day-to-day failure.

Stephen Webster 00:12

That’s Dr Alena Vdovchenko, a postdoctoral scientist at Imperial College London, talking in April this year at the Failure in Science conference.

Alena Vdovchenko 00:22

In the lab, simply most of the things don’t work the way you plan them.

So sometimes you carefully design the experiment. You run it for sometimes weeks, months. It depends.

Maybe days if you’re lucky.

But then when you analyze the results, you realize that okay, you didn’t account for factor A.

So then you have to go back.

You need to redesign the experiment, maybe read more literature, go back to the lab.

Stephen Webster 00:48

Alena was speaking at the session called A Taxonomy of Failure, where we heard early career researchers explaining how, in real life, (let’s put it like this), things often don’t go quite as planned.

Alena Vdovchenko 01:01

But overall, I think a lot of chemistry is trial and error. And during my PhD, we have that quote printed in our lab.

Theory is when you know everything but nothing works.

Practice is when everything works but no one knows why.

In our lab, theory and practice are combined.

Nothing works, and no one knows why.

I feel like it’s very funny, but also very uncomfortably true.

Stephen Webster 01:30

I’m Dr Stephen Webster, director of the Good Science Project at Imperial College London, a programme that examines what we like about research culture, and what we don’t.

And in episode two, we hear panelist Melanie Stefan, professor of physiology at Berlin Medical School, talk about failure and the lab.

Melanie Stefan 01:57

My first big experience of failure in science was when I was doing my masters in a developmental biology lab, and I really had a difficult time there.

I didn’t quite know how to troubleshoot experiments if they failed. I didn’t quite understand what I was doing. I think it was not the right place for me.

And the worst day was when my supervisor called me into his office and said, "Melanie, I think you should really look for jobs outside of science."

And that was devastating because I had been studying science for many years at the time. I saw myself as a scientist. I didn’t really have a Plan B.

So much of my identity was being a scientist and doing science.

Not just that I loved doing it, and I was really interested in it, but also I didn’t know what else I could do.

So this was really a devastating failure for me.

And I wrote an article about this in Nature. It’s also the only thing I have published in Nature.

Other journals exist, and since then I’ve kind of become the poster child of failure, kind of without intending it.

So at the Failure in Science conference at Imperial College, I talked about this article I wrote called A CV of Failures.

And the story of that is after my master’s degree, (which I ended up completing in the end), I did a PhD, and I had a very great time there.

I had a lot of fun. It was quite a successful time for me.

But then I was done with that, and I needed to apply for funding to go to the next stage of my career as a postdoc.

And it was really hard. It was really hard to find funding. And I was rejected from, a lot of my funding applications were rejected. I started doubting myself.

And I also thought that, "Oh my God, I’m the first person this has happenened to."

Because all the other scientists around me, obviously, or like the scientists who were like a bit further ahead they were further ahead because they were ultimately successful in securing a postdoc position.

And so all I saw around me was ultimately the successes.

So I felt like I was the only one who had ever failed. So that made it even worse, and so this gave me the idea of writing this article calling for a CV of failures.

So the idea would be that the successful people in science would actually open up about their failures that they had on their way, and how many jobs they didn’t get, how many positions they weren’t admitted to, how many grants they failed to receive, how many papers were rejected, things like that.

So that younger scientists like I was at the time could actually take heart and see that this is actually a normal part of the process and that they’re not alone.

So that was the idea. And since then, I’ve kind of become the poster child of failure a little bit.

A lot of friends tell me, "Oh, Melanie, I read something about failure. I was thinking of you."

I was like, "Thank you. That is so nice."

I think it’s generally really cool that there has been following up on this article a bigger discussion about failure in science that the conference was also part of.

I think that’s really lovely. And it’s really lovely to see people come together and talk about this concept.

Melanie Stefan 05:43

The conference is called Failure in Science, but I’d like to smuggle in engineering. I know Mary already mentioned engineering in the last session, and I’m an engineer, and I think engineering has a very well developed tradition of understanding and learning from failure.

Melanie Stefan 06:03

So I liked the the session that was called "A View from the Lab.

And it was especially nice to to hear from the more junior scientists about how they interacted with failure and how they experienced it.

But I also thought the moderator George Constantinides is one thing that really that I found really interesting about what he said was how he compared it to engineering.

George Constantinides 06:27

And I think if I were to summarize the very broad literature on failure in engineering, at least my understanding is: number one, there is no failure without uncertainty.

And number two, structured ways from learning from failure are essential.

And I think those are things that we can carry forward into many different aspects of our work.

In general, I would kind of summarize by saying, in my view, if we want people to fly high, then we have to make it easy and safe to fail well.

Melanie Stefan 07:02

And in engineering, you have to fail. Like, that’s how. You build something, you try a prototype and then it fails, and you learn from that.

You watch how exactly it failed, you analyze it, and then you build the next better version, and the next version, the next version.

And I think the point he was making, and I really agree with that, is that we should treat scientific careers in the same way, and that we need to give people spaces where it’s safe to try something and fail, and then to talk about it, and learn from it, and then do better the next time and try again.

And maybe fail in a different way, but then build something in the end that’s better. So I really like that engineering analogy.

So one thing that also came up in a lot of the discussions at the conference, and that I think is really important, is the question of who actually gets to talk about failure and who gets to fail.

So the reason why I’m invited to conferences like that is that ultimately I did finish my master’s degree, and ultimately I did become a scientist.

And this is why I get to talk about failure is in my scientific career is because ultimately I have succeeded.

And what about the people, though, who have failed?

And I use the word advisedly.

It’s not always like a personal failure.

But people who have set out to have a life in science and are now doing something else. We never hear from them, right, because they are not in that space anymore?

So I think it takes a certain amount of privilege and position to be allowed to talk about failure.

And also, when I was a young scientist and I was looking for positions, I was sometimes, like, googling my name, and then the first thing that came up was A CV of Failures.

And I thought that was really strategically not that clever of me.

But I was not in a position then where it was much less safe to open up about failures.

And now I’m in a position where I can do it because I have a professorship. Nothing is nothing bad is going to happen to me.

So this privilege of opening up about failure is really important.

And then also failure itself is something that you need quite a bit of privilege to do.

So for me, I was able to apply for several postdoc grants and failed to get them until there was finally one that I succeeded in getting.

I was in a position to do that because my institute was happy to pay me for another year after I finished my PhD, and my supervisor was happy to keep me around in the lab, and my visa status didn’t depend on me securing funding right away.

So, and I didn’t have family to take care of at that time.

So it’s really like a lot of privileges came together that allowed me to even fail that much.

And that’s also something we need to think about. Who gets to fail? And then who gets to talk about failure.

I always had this kind of secret plan B, which was to open a cinema.

And I think a lot of my friends in science, if you ask them, they always have like a secret plan B. And it’s usually to do with doing something lovely like opening a bakery or opening a bike shop.

And for me it was opening a cinema, a small indie cinema.

I don’t know if I would have done it actually if I left science. But it was kind of a nice fantasy to escape to, and it sometimes still is.

But I still think, "Oh, I can open a cinema if if everything else fails."

But I would not think of it as a failure.

Because I think there’s a lot of ways to leave science, or to leave academia, and do really interesting and really cool things.

So a lot of my friends who were at university with me are not practicing scientists anymore. Or at least not research scientists, but they do really cool things in industry, in education, in all kinds of sectors.

So this view of leaving science as a failure, I think, is quite problematic as well.

I think it’s really important to share failures as well, in order to distinguish what is a personal failure and what is a system failing you.

And if I submit a grant application and I don’t get the grant, that’s fine.

That might be that my idea wasn’t good enough. Or the grant wasn’t well enough thought out.

But if 100 of my friends submit grant applications and then only 10 of them, only five of them, get a grant, then that maybe points to there being not enough money for research or not enough funding.

And I think we need to open up about failures as well to see where there are places in the system where the system actually could be improved.

rss_8_1793053621.title: Brazil election: many scientists relieved as Lula wins surprise victory
rss_8_1793053621.text:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva celebrated on the evening of 25 October after coming from behind to win re-election as Brazil’s president.Credit: Maira Erlich/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won his bid for re-election on 25 October, to the relief of many scientists who feared for the future of Brazilian research if right-wing candidate Flávio Bolsonaro prevailed.

In recent weeks, some of Brazil’s leading scientific organizations, including the Brazilian Academy of Sciences in Rio de Janeiro, circulated an open letter endorsing Lula, a leftist former labour leader. It received more than 20,000 signatures. “It’s hard to express just how happy the scientific community and the Brazilian society is with Lula’s victory,” says Paulo Artaxo, a physicist at the University of São Paulo.

Science philanthropy is rising in Brazil ― upending a long tradition

Many worried that, if Bolsonaro were elected, he might slash support for Brazilian science and undermine it in the way that his father, Jair Bolsonaro, did. Jair was Brazil’s president from 2019 to 2023, and during that time, he cut science funding and expressed anti-science rhetoric during the COVID-19 pandemic, casting doubt on vaccines and promoting unproven treatments. The former president could not run for office again because he was sentenced to prison over a coup plot that he instigated after he lost his bid for re-election to Lula in 2022. He is currently serving the sentence at home because of health concerns.

It was a surprise victory yesterday for Lula, who won 51.8% of the vote compared with Flávio Bolsonaro’s 48.2%. During the first round of voting on 4 October, Lula finished behind Bolsonaro, but because neither candidate earned 50% of the total votes, a second round of voting was required. “It was very moving to watch this historic turnaround,” says Sidarta Ribeiro, a neuroscientist at the Federal University of Rio Grande do Norte in Natal.

Lula’s victory came at the end of a tumultuous election day. Shortly before the polls were meant to close, a justice in Brazil’s Supreme Court ordered them to remain open for an additional two hours. The move was requested by both Lula’s and Bolsonaro’s campaigns because of public transportation problems that made it difficult for voters to reach polling stations. In a short speech yesterday, Bolsonaro said he would not accept the results.

Support for science

This will be Lula’s fourth term overall as president of Brazil, a record for the country. He initially led Brazil for two terms between 2003 and 2011. During those terms and his current term, which started in 2023, he championed the expansion of federal universities and efforts to make higher education accessible to a broad range of Brazilians, support that he has pledged to continue. He also launched a program in 2024 that brought back about 600 Brazilian scientists to the country from international institutions, where some had gone seeking improved funding and resources.

“Lula said very clearly in his victory speech that we need to strengthen federal universities and federal institutes and significantly improve how we prepare young people for a new world of [artificial intelligence] and robotics,” Ribeiro says.

Supporters of Brazilian President Lula cheered in the streets of São Paulo on 25 October after it became clear that he had won his bid for re-election in a tight race.Credit: Rodrigo Paiva/Getty

Flávio Bolsonaro had pledged to transfer operation of Brazil’s 69 federal universities from the Ministry of Education to the Ministry of Science and Technology, which has a much smaller budget. In addition, he said he would emphasize applied sciences over basic research, which concerned some in the scientific community because “the countries that have made the greatest advances in science are those with an extremely strong foundation in basic research”, Ribeiro says.

Another major source of concern for some researchers about the election was the future of Brazil’s environmental policies. Under President Lula, deforestation in Brazil’s considerable portion of the Amazon rainforest fell to its lowest level since measurements began in 1988. Between 2019 and 2023, however, deforestation rose by almost 60% under Jair Bolsonaro, and a similar trend was expected under his son. The Amazon rainforest is considered one of the world’s largest carbon sinks, but studies suggest that increasing deforestation could cause it to release more carbon than it absorbs.

Meanwhile, Lula said during his recent campaign that he is committed to ending deforestation in Brazil by 2030, and that he would cut the country’s greenhouse-gas emissions in line with the Paris Agreement, which nations signed onto nearly a decade ago to curb climate change. “Lula’s government plan is very clear: he’ll work towards zero deforestation in the Amazon and towards implementing energy transition programs that end the use of fossil fuels in Brazil,” Artaxo says.

rss_9_1793053623.title: ctDNA clearance and outcomes for resectable lung cancer from NeoCOAST-2
rss_9_1793053623.text: Patients with resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remain at high risk of relapse despite perioperative treatment1-3. NeoCOAST-2 (NCT05061550), a phase 2, randomised platform trial, tested novel perioperative treatments in patients with stage IIA–IIIB NSCLC. At primary analysis, combining standard chemotherapy plus durvalumab (anti-PD-L1 antibody) with oleclumab (Arm 1, n = 76), monalizumab (Arm 2, n = 72) or datopotamab deruxtecan (Dato-DXd; Arm 4, n = 54) resulted in pathological complete response (pCR) rates of 20.3%, 25.7%, and 35.2%, respectively4. Here, we present the first report of prespecified secondary endpoints of event-free survival (EFS) and circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) clearance, and exploratory analyses of associations between ctDNA dynamics and clinical outcomes. The 24-month EFS rates were 70.5%, 75.7% and 77.9% in Arms 1, 2 and 4, respectively. Using a tumour-agnostic assay, ctDNA clearance at neoadjuvant Cycle 3 Day 1 was highest in Arm 4 (50.9%, 54.5%, and 72.5% in each arm, respectively). ctDNA clearance correlated with prolonged EFS versus non-clearance (pooled hazard ratio (HR) 0.22; 95% CI = 0.11–0.45, P = 0.0000443). Patients with both ctDNA clearance and pCR had favourable EFS outcomes versus those with neither (EFS HR 0.10, 95% CI = 0.02–0.42, P = 0.002). These findings suggest combined assessment of ctDNA clearance and pCR may improve risk stratification, and that the numerically highest pCR4 and EFS rates with the Dato-DXd combination warrant further evaluation.

rss_11_1793053625.title: Elusive snow leopards and evasive particles: Books in brief
rss_11_1793053625.text:
Wonders of the Quantum World

Danni Holmes Melbourne Univ. Press (2026)

“If a fully-fledged quantum computer arrived on our doorstep today, it would be like giving a caveman a smartphone,” writes physicist Danni Holmes. Her first book is a sparkling analysis of the quantum world. It takes the non-physicist reader through the laws of classical physics discovered by Isaac Newton and James Clerk Maxwell to more-recent fascinating facets of the field, such as the reason why black holes don’t last forever and whether human consciousness could have a quantum origin.

The Age of Cures

Barry Werth Simon & Schuster (2026)

Any study of the US pharmaceutical industry involves finance as well as science, as journalist Barry Werth unpacked in his first book, The Billion-Dollar Molecule. His latest book discusses the United States’ “eighty-year-long preeminence in drug research”, which began during the Second World War under the direction of presidential science adviser Vannevar Bush. Focusing on Bush and five post-war leaders in the field of pharmacology, such as Max Tishler, Werth illuminates the value of long-term investment in science.

Divination Engines

Xiaochang Li Univ. Chicago Press (2026)

Communication researcher Xiaochang Li describes her complex book as a cultural history of both technology and communication. It analyses “how words became data, how data became imperative, and how the problem of language came to shape the very foundations of algorithmic culture” — including for large language models and artificial intelligence. Li recounts vigorous debates between linguists, computer scientists and communication engineers, triggered by the thorny relationship between speech and writing.

The Matter of Architecture

Paul Dobraszczyk Reaktion (2026)
